content: The difference in intake levels between the lowest and highest trans-fatty acid (TFA) consumption was insufficient to allow for reliable comparisons. Additionally, in the limited studies that assessed low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, the highest levels of ruminant TFA intake were similar to those observed for industrially produced and total TFA. Separate analyses were conducted for total, industrially produced, and ruminant TFA in the meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies, as most studies did not differentiate between industrially produced and ruminant TFA, reporting only total TFA intake. For the regression analysis of total TFA, all trials assessing total, industrially produced, or ruminant TFA intake were included in a single analysis. The effects of industrially produced and ruminant TFA on all-cause mortality and cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) were derived from studies where dietary intake was assessed using tissue measurements. Although the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health raised concerns about assessing dietary saturated fatty acid (SFA) intake via tissue measurements, the correlation between TFA levels in tissue and dietary intake has generally been shown to be stronger. The effects of industrially produced and ruminant TFA on coronary heart disease were based on studies where dietary intake was self-reported. It was concluded that the available evidence did not support making a distinction between industrially produced and ruminant TFA. Since the majority of studies included in systematic reviews reported results for total TFA intake (encompassing both industrially produced and ruminant sources), it was deemed appropriate to consider only total TFA evidence when formulating recommendations on TFA intake. Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), a specific type of TFA with a unique three-dimensional structure, was included in the systematic review and regression analyses of blood lipids. However, the number of trials assessing CLA was limited, and intake levels were very low. The results of these trials did not indicate that CLA had a significantly different effect on blood lipids compared to other TFAs when consumed at similar levels. Consequently, the NUGAG Subgroup concluded that CLA, as a contributor to total TFA intake, should be included in the definition of TFA used in the recommendations. This approach was further supported by unpublished studies identified during an informal literature update. These included two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showing that diets enriched with ruminant TFA significantly raised LDL cholesterol compared to both a control diet and a diet enriched with industrially produced TFA. A 2020 systematic review of RCTs also concluded that ruminant TFA caused greater increases in LDL cholesterol than industrially produced TFA. While many studies on CLA supplements have been published, the amounts provided in supplements are generally much higher than those naturally consumed in foods, and assessing this separate body of evidence was beyond the scope of the guideline. In translating evidence into recommendations, the NUGAG Subgroup considered the certainty of the evidence, the desirable and undesirable effects of interventions, the priority of the problem being addressed, values and preferences related to the interventions, feasibility and acceptability of implementation, potential impacts on equity and human rights, and the cost of available options for public health officials and program managers. Since the recommended interventions in this guideline are dietary goals, they can be translated into policies and actions in various ways, such as behavior change interventions, fiscal policies, marketing regulations, labeling schemes, and reformulation of manufactured products. The overall certainty in the evidence for lower versus higher SFA intake was assessed as moderate. For consuming SFA at less than 10% of total energy intake compared to more than 10%, the certainty was assessed as low. For replacing SFA with different nutrients, the certainty was assessed as moderate for plant-based monounsaturated fatty acids, low for polyunsaturated fatty acids and other sources, and very low for free sugars and high-glycemic-index foods. The overall certainty in the evidence for lower versus higher TFA intake was assessed as moderate. For consuming TFA at less than 1% of total energy intake compared to more than 1%, the certainty was assessed as low. For replacing TFA with different nutrients, the certainty was moderate for carbohydrates, low for plant-based monounsaturated fatty acids, and very low for polyunsaturated fatty acids, animal-based monounsaturated fatty acids, free sugars, and high-glycemic-index foods. There was robust evidence for cardiovascular benefits of reducing SFA and TFA intake across various study types and outcomes, as well as evidence for reduced risk of all-cause mortality from prospective observational studies. No adverse effects were associated with reducing SFA or TFA intake when assessed in aggregate. Although an increased risk of type 2 diabetes was associated with reduced intake of two specific odd-chain SFAs (pentadecanoic acid and heptadecanoic acid), these findings were based on tissue measurements, which may not consistently distinguish between dietary intake and endogenous synthesis. Furthermore, SFAs are typically consumed as mixtures in foods, and reducing overall SFA intake is associated with reduced risk of all-cause mortality and CVDs. Concerns about the potential negative impact of reducing dietary fat intake on nutritional adequacy and growth in children were addressed. The systematic review did not identify undesirable effects on linear growth and development in children who reduced their SFA intake. Two large studies, the Dietary Intervention Study in Children (DISC) and the Special Turku Coronary Risk Factor Intervention Project (STRIP), concluded that a diet low in SFA did not affect normal growth and development in children and was therefore safe. The STRIP study demonstrated the long-term safety of a low-SFA diet, with no adverse effects on growth, neurological or sexual development, or psychosocial well-being over more than 20 years of follow-up. Although no evidence was identified for the effects of reducing TFA intake in children, concerns about limiting ruminant TFA found in dairy and meat were addressed through modeling analyses. The WHO recommendations on SFA and TFA intake allow for adequate consumption of dairy foods, particularly reduced-fat versions, and align with many national guidelines on dairy intake. Reducing SFA and TFA intake in children reduces CVD risk without any identified adverse effects, and the desirable effects strongly outweigh the undesirable effects. Global efforts to eliminate industrially produced TFA are well underway, supported by the WHO REPLACE action package. As of September 2022, 60 countries had implemented mandatory TFA limits, with 43 adopting best-practice policies that virtually eliminate industrially produced TFA or ban partially hydrogenated oils.
